findings.text: Guest abort tail completes a data or instruction fault after earlier decoding. It first resolves any active nested stage-two translation into a host-visible intermediate address, then maps that address through the guest frame to host mapping, then dispatches to cache-maintenance skip, input-output emulation, access-flag handling, or protected versus normal memory fault handling, always releasing the read-side critical section before returning handled, retry, or injected-abort status.

When the current hardware MMU is a nested stage-two context with nesting enabled, the handler attempts a nested walk, treats a transient retry as handled without injection, converts walk or permission failures into a synthesized fault delivered to the nested hypervisor, and otherwise continues using the translated output plus retained nested context for later accounting.

If the host mapping is missing or a write targets a read-only slot, instruction faults take a synchronous external abort injection path, stage-one table-walk faults take a data abort injection path, cache-maintenance accesses to unmapped ranges advance the guest program counter as handled, and remaining cases merge the high intermediate bits with low fault-address bits before delegating to input-output abort handling.

Valid host mappings are checked against the physical address limit, access-flag faults are completed by a dedicated handler as handled, and other faults build a common descriptor carrying vCPU, original fault address, nested context, slot and host address, dispatching to a protected-VM path when the VM is protected and otherwise to guest-memory versus normal user-memory handlers, normalizing zero to handled and mapping execute denial to instruction-abort injection.

Nested stage-two permission evaluation and fault injection are available to other compilation units operating on a vCPU plus translation state, returning whether the fault should be forwarded and delivering a supplied exception syndrome to the nested hypervisor after restoring fault address state.

Permission evaluation starts with a cleared syndrome and reports benign when the trap is not a permission fault. Instruction cases consult execute rights selected by current privilege, data cases compare fault direction against readable and writable attributes, and a violation records a permission fault syndrome for the recorded translation level.
Nested fault syndromes preserve the current vCPU exception syndrome except for the fault-status field, which is replaced by a value computed from translation level and requested fault code.

Guest-frame range unmapping and young-bit test with optional clear are exported for memory-management callbacks operating on a VM plus frame interval, reporting a boolean continuation or young status.

All three range operations report false without action when stage-two tables are absent or the VM is protected. Unmapping removes the corresponding intermediate range and additionally clears nested shadow state while still reporting false; ageing queries the stage-two young state over the same range, clearing on age and preserving on test.

Host hypervisor page-table operations allocate a zeroed host page for table storage and delegate reference management and address conversion to host helpers, providing the allocation, reference, and translation hooks required by generic page-table code.

Memory-region commit, prepare, free, generation notification, and shadow flush are exported for the generic memory-slot lifecycle, validating and applying host and guest mapping consequences of creation, movement, flag change, and deletion.

Commit applies dirty-logging consequences after the slot is installed: deletion with logging enabled does nothing, manual-protect mode defers work to later clears, otherwise the region is write-protected and split for fine tracking; when logging is not enabled any cached split pages are released, covering creation, movement, deletion, and flag-only paths.

Prepare rejects protected-VM slot deletion or movement after creation and rejects dirty-log or read-only flags on protected VMs. It bounds the new region by the VM physical size, requires guest-memory slots to be private-only, forbids guest-memory with memory tagging, and scans host virtual areas covering the region to enforce tagging allowance, forbid dirty logging on direct-mapping areas, and allow cacheable direct mappings only with hardware support.
Shadow flush for a slot holds the VM address-space lock for writing while removing the slot intermediate range from stage-two tables and clearing nested shadow state.
Set-way-flush and cache-toggle helpers are exported for trap handling when guest cache maintenance or enablement changes, adjusting stage-two flushing and virtualization trap controls plus tracing.

The first set-way operation with virtualization trapping disabled flushes the whole VM and enables trapping; later operations rely on trapping until caches disable. Toggling compares prior and current cache enablement, flushing on any change, clearing trapping once caches are on, and tracing the transition with program counter and states.

Virtualized nested control register translation cache holds the guest virtual address under translation, stage-one walk parameters and result, resolved host physical address plus a writability flag, a CPU affinity marker set to negative when unmapped, and a validity flag that may only change under the address-space lock for writing.
The number of nested stage-two address-space structures reserved per virtual CPU is two.
Nested stage-two walk parameters carry a base address, maximum output address width, page shift, starting level, table size selector, and flags for endianness and hardware access-flag handling.
Translation-control to granule conversion yields a power-of-two page size derived from the corresponding shift helper for the given VM and control value.
Guest mapping size-hint lookup requires the VM address-space lock held for writing and must be called with that protection.

Size-hint lookup seeds a tag from the current granule, treating unknown granules as the largest size, then iteratively aligns the target address to progressively larger block candidates per granule, consulting shadow stage-two leaves for validity and embedded level, and returns the combined tag only when the resulting extent covers the original address, otherwise zero.

Invalidation extent uses the operand tag when present and the range-hint feature is available, otherwise consults shadow state for a hint, converts the tag to a byte size, and on zero falls back to a granule-specific maximum of one gigabyte, thirty-two megabytes, or five-hundred-twelve megabytes, warning if no size results.

Iteration over nested address spaces by virtual machine identifier holds the VM address-space lock for writing, skips invalid entries, and invokes the supplied callback only on entries whose table identifier matches.

Stage-one invalidation scope is a discriminated record distinguishing full, address-specific, address-all-identifier, and identifier-only operations, carrying an identifier plus address and length used according to the discriminator.

Virtualized register invalidation always advances the VM invalidation sequence with ordering even when no entry matches, to account for concurrent walks and break-before-make sequences, then walks all cached translations and discards entries matching the scope: all entries for full scope, overlap plus identifier check for non-global address scope, overlap alone for all-identifier address scope, and non-global plus identifier match for identifier scope.

Stage-one invalidation decoding groups operations into full, address, identifier, address-all-identifier, and range families across shareability and notification variants, deriving address and length from operand tag sizing with alignment and sign extension for direct forms and from a range decoder yielding address, length, and optionally identifier for range forms.

Top-level stage-one invalidation for nested execution computes the scope without locks then holds the VM address-space lock for writing while applying virtualized-register invalidation, which itself asserts write protection.
Nested invalidation-range computation, iteration by identifier, stage-one invalidation handling, and full shadow flush are exported for trap and teardown paths.
Full shadow teardown expects no active references on each nested address space, warning otherwise, and still proceeds to release page tables and uninitialize nested state.

Virtualized register translation follows invalidate, walk, fault-in, and publish phases: it first discards any cached entry and prepares walk parameters under write protection, then walks the guest address under read-side protection, faults the resulting frame through guest-memory or normal paths, validates mappability, and finally publishes the translation under write protection unless a concurrent invalidation forces retry.

Translation uses read-side protection for the guest walk and fault-in, write protection for initial invalidation plus walk preparation and for final publication, a sequence snapshot with barrier to detect concurrent invalidation, and a negative CPU marker plus mapping request on successful publish with conditional dirty accounting.

Missing slots or unmappable frames fail the stage-one walk as external aborts, guest-memory failures produce a memory-fault exit for userspace, write intent follows the original fault direction with read-only slots reported non-writable, and successful writable mappings are released with dirty tracking and marked dirty in the VM.

Virtualized register permission handling promotes a write to a read-only host mapping despite stage-one writable permission to an external abort, otherwise injecting a permission fault that uses the guest translation level rather than the host level.

Known limits in these paths include no support for the largest intermediate address width in nested invalidation, deferred nested young-bit handling noted for later work, an acknowledged overly strict mappability check for direct mappings, and defensive checks that trap out-of-bounds intermediate addresses and unexpected non-permission fault kinds.
